title: Kestra keeps execution history in its own mutable backend, so an approval inside a pipeline has nowhere to live
content:
Kestra orchestrates data workflows and keeps its execution history in its own backend, which is mutable. That history is about runs: which task executed, when, with what status. It is the operational record of the pipeline, not a record of the business events that occur inside it.

The research names the missing object exactly — 'this figure was approved, by this person' has nowhere to live. An orchestrator can encode the approval as a step and can show that the step completed, but the completion is a row it owns and can rewrite, and preserving the meaning of the approval is not what an orchestrator is built to do.

For conapi, which delivers Kestra-based pipelines, this is the seam. The pipeline is already the place where the approval happens, so dispatching that moment as a typed operation moves the business event out of the mutable execution log and into a record that outlives the run it came from.
